Darius the Third. Ruling from three hundred thirty-six to three hundred thirty BCE, Darius the Third was the last king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, facing the unprecedented challenge of Alexander the Great's invasion. Though he inherited a vast and wealthy empire, Darius the Third was unable to marshal effective resistance to Alexander's military genius and was ultimately defeated in three decisive battles, ending over two centuries of Persian imperial supremacy and reshaping the ancient world.

Darius the Third ascended to the Persian throne in three hundred thirty-six BCE as a junior member of the Achaemenid dynasty, a period when internal political instability had weakened the empire's cohesion and military readiness. Alexander the Great invaded Persia in three hundred thirty-four BCE with roughly thirty-five thousand troops. Darius the Third commanded vastly larger armies but faced strategic challenges in coordinating his empire's forces and countering Alexander's tactical innovations.

Three major battles between Darius and Alexander defined the campaign: the Granicus River in three hundred thirty-four BCE, Issus in three hundred thirty-three BCE, and Gaugamela in three hundred thirty-one BCE. Each battle was a decisive defeat that progressively weakened Persian resistance. At Gaugamela, the final and most decisive battle, Darius commanded perhaps one million troops—likely an exaggeration by ancient sources—against Alexander's roughly forty-seven thousand. Alexander's maneuvering routed the Persian forces despite their numerical superiority.

Darius fled the battlefield at Gaugamela and was assassinated by Bessus, a satrap or provincial governor, in three hundred thirty BCE while attempting to raise new forces. His death marked the effective end of Achaemenid rule. The swift collapse of the Persian Empire was shocking to contemporaries: an empire that had dominated the ancient world for two centuries fell to a young Macedonian general and his army within four years. Modern historians note that Darius faced an unprecedented military challenge and that his defeat reflects Alexander's exceptional generalship rather than Darius's incompetence.
